rewritten_text: Mr. Attorney-General wished to acquaint the jury with the fact that the accused before them, though youthful in age, was experienced in those treasonous practices for which his life must be forfeited. That his communications with the national enemy had not begun today, yesterday, last year, or even the year preceding it. That the prisoner had certainly been travelling back and forth between England and France for a longer period, conducting secret affairs for which no honest explanation could be offered. That, were treachery capable of prospering—which, fortunately, it never was—the true guilt and depravity of these dealings might have escaped detection. That Providence had instead inspired a person above both fear and reproach to investigate the prisoner's designs and, horrified by his discoveries, reveal them to his Majesty's Chief Secretary of State and most honourable Privy Council. That this patriot would appear before the jury. That his conduct and position were, taken together, sublime. That he had formerly been the prisoner's friend; but, discovering his disgrace in an hour at once fortunate and unhappy, had determined to sacrifice upon his country's sacred altar the traitor he could no longer hold dear. That, were Britain to award statues to public benefactors as ancient Rome and Greece had done, this exemplary citizen would certainly receive one. That, since Britain did not make such awards, he probably would not. That Virtue, as the poets had remarked in numerous passages which he was certain the jury knew word for word—at which the jurors' expressions betrayed a guilty awareness of knowing none of them—was in some degree infectious, particularly that radiant virtue called patriotism, or love of one's country. That the exalted example of this spotless and irreproachable Crown witness, whom it was an honour even inadequately to mention, had spread to the prisoner's servant, awakening in him a sacred resolve to inspect his master's desk drawers and pockets and secretly take his papers. That he, Mr. Attorney-General, expected attempts to discredit this excellent servant; nevertheless, he generally preferred the man to his own brothers and sisters, and held him in greater esteem than his own father and mother. That he confidently invited the jury to feel the same. That these two witnesses' testimony, together with the documents they had uncovered and which would be presented, would establish that the prisoner had obtained lists of his Majesty's forces, their stations, and their preparations on land and sea, leaving no question that he had regularly passed this intelligence to an enemy power.

He could not stop himself. And it infuriated him to think that Becky Thatcher seemed entirely unaware he was even alive. Yet she did notice him, and she knew she was winning. She was pleased to see him suffer as she had suffered.

Amy's cheerful chatter became unbearable. Tom dropped hints about things he had to attend to, urgent things, and how quickly time was passing. It was no use; the girl kept chirping away. ‘Oh, damn her,’ Tom thought. ‘Am I ever going to get rid of her?’ At last he insisted that he had to deal with those matters. She innocently told him she would be ‘around’ when school finished, and he hurried off, hating her for saying it.

‘Any other boy!’ Tom thought, grinding his teeth. ‘Any boy in town except that Saint Louis show-off who thinks he's so well dressed and such an aristocrat! All right, mister. I beat you the first day you ever came here, and I'll beat you again. Just wait until I catch you outside! I'll take you and—’

He acted out a fight with an imaginary boy, punching the air, kicking, and gouging. ‘Oh, you will, will you? Now you're shouting you've had enough? Well, let that teach you!’ And he finished the imaginary beating to his satisfaction.

At noon, Tom ran home. His conscience could endure no more of Amy's grateful delight, and his jealousy could stand no more of the other torment. Becky went back to looking at pictures with Alfred. But as the minutes crept by without Tom appearing to suffer, her triumph began to fade, and she lost interest. She grew serious, then distracted, then miserable. Two or three times she listened eagerly to approaching footsteps, but each hope proved false: Tom did not come. At last she felt utterly unhappy and wished she had not taken things so far. Poor Alfred could see that he was losing her attention but had no idea why. He kept crying, ‘Oh, here's a good one! Look at this!’ Finally she lost patience. ‘Oh, stop bothering me! I don't care about them!’ She burst into tears, stood up, and walked away.

Alfred came alongside her, intending to offer comfort, but she said:

‘Can't you go away and leave me alone? I hate you!’

The boy stopped, wondering what he had done. She had promised to look at pictures throughout the lunch break, after all. She went on walking and crying. Alfred wandered thoughtfully into the empty schoolhouse, humiliated and angry. It was easy enough to work out the truth: she had simply used him to take revenge on Tom Sawyer.

The exquisitely refined gentlemen wore little dangling ornaments that jingled as they moved languidly about. Their golden chains chimed like tiny, costly bells. Between that chiming and the rustle of silk, brocade, and fine linen, the air stirred enough to waft Saint Antoine and his ravenous hunger far away.

Clothing was the one reliable charm that kept everything in its proper place. Everyone was dressed for a costume ball that would never end. From the Tuileries Palace, through Monseigneur and the entire Court, through the Chambers, the law courts, and every level of society except the scarecrows, this costume ball extended down to the public executioner. To preserve the spell, he was required to perform his duties with curled and powdered hair, a coat trimmed in gold lace, light shoes, and white silk stockings. In this delicate outfit he presided over the gallows and the breaking wheel; the axe was rarely used. His fellow practitioners in the provinces—Monsieur Orleans and the rest—called him Monsieur Paris, following the bishops' custom of taking names from their cities. And who at Monseigneur's reception in that year of Our Lord, seventeen hundred and eighty, could conceivably doubt that a system founded on a hangman in curls, powder, gold lace, elegant shoes, and white silk stockings would outlast the stars themselves?

Having relieved his four attendants of their burdens and drunk his chocolate, Monseigneur ordered the doors of his innermost sanctuary opened and emerged. What submission followed, what grovelling and flattery, what servility and abject humiliation! His guests bowed so completely in body and spirit that they had nothing left to offer Heaven, which may help explain why Monseigneur's worshippers never troubled it.

Granting a promising word here and a smile there, a whisper to one fortunate slave and a gesture to another, Monseigneur moved graciously through his rooms toward the distant outer boundary of Truth. There he turned and retraced his steps until, in due course, the spirits who served his chocolate shut him back inside his sanctuary, and he appeared no more.

With the performance finished, the fluttering air grew into a little storm, and the expensive bells went jingling down the stairs. Soon only one person remained of the entire crowd. With his hat tucked under his arm and his snuffbox in his hand, he moved slowly among the mirrors toward the exit.

‘I consign you,’ he said, pausing at the final doorway and turning toward the sanctuary, ‘to the Devil!’

Then he shook the snuff off his fingers as though shaking dust from his feet, and went quietly downstairs.
